bot.cientifico.invernadero: If you cut the greenhouse power, we will run out of food and fresh air tomorrow.
bot.cientifico.2: The greenhouse plants are getting cold. Give them power so they keep making oxygen!
bot.cientifico.3: Without light in the greenhouse, our Martian crops won't grow today.
bot.ingeniero.blindaje: If we don't reinforce the shelter shield today, there won't be time when the storm hits.
bot.ingeniero.2: The shelter shielding is still low. I need power in the panels to charge it in time!
bot.ingeniero.3: The solar storm is getting closer and the shelter still needs more protection.
bot.medico.dosis: Radiation falls on Mars every day. Give power to the med bay so I can keep the crew healthy.
bot.medico.2: The medical monitors need power to track how much radiation the crew is taking.
bot.medico.3: The crew has already taken a lot of radiation. Power up the med bay to protect them!
panelModulo.desc.invernadero: The greenhouse provides food and oxygen for the crew.
panelModulo.desc.energia: Solar panels charge the shelter's radiation shielding.
panelModulo.desc.refugio: Protects the crew during the solar storm.
panelModulo.desc.comunicaciones: Watches the Sun to give an early warning before the storm.
panelModulo.desc.enfermeria: Cares for the crew and tracks their radiation dose.
reporte.dosisIntro: Radiation dose received by your crew in the simulation:
reporte.curiosity: A real solar storm reached Mars on May 20, 2024. Nobody lived there: Curiosity measured a dose that NASA says would have been about 8,100 µGy for a person standing next to the rover, equivalent to around 30 chest X-rays. This is a historical reference, not a measurement of your crew.
reporte.pronostico: The coronal mass ejection of {fecha} was real. The forecast of its arrival near Earth was off by {horas} hours. This is an Earth observation, not a forecast for Mars.
reporte.pronosticoNoDisponible: There is not enough data to compare this event's forecast.
reporte.consejo: One idea to explore: prepare the shielding and get the crew to the shelter early, because storms can arrive sooner than expected.
fuentes.introduccion: The mission uses historical data and an imaginary base. Explore where each idea comes from.
fuentes.donki.texto: DONKI is NASA's database of space weather events, including coronal mass ejections. The game uses historical events stored locally.
fuentes.scoreboard.texto: The Earth CME Scoreboard compares forecasts with arrivals observed near Earth. The game uses those timings for its challenge; they are not arrivals measured at Mars. Some event associations are provisional.
fuentes.scoreboard.enlace: Learn about the Earth CME Scoreboard
fuentes.curiosity.texto: During the solar storm of May 20, 2024, Curiosity measured radiation on Mars. NASA estimates a person standing next to the rover would have received about 8,100 micrograys, or around 30 chest X-rays.
fuentes.curiosity.enlace: Read about Curiosity and the storm
fuentes.sol.texto: A Martian day, or sol, lasts about 24 hours and 39 minutes. The game rounds it to 24.65 hours.
fuentes.sol.enlace: Read about the length of a sol
fuentes.chapea.texto: CHAPEA is a NASA simulation on Earth with four people living in a habitat that imitates a Mars mission. Its roles include command, engineering, medicine and science; the game's crew is fictional.
fuentes.simplificado.texto: Energy, life support, shielding and crew doses use game rules and values. They are not NASA measurements or predictions. The base and its characters are imaginary.
inicio.subtitulo: You are the commander of a base on Mars. A solar storm is coming and the forecast isn't exact. When do you protect your crew?
inicio.honestidad: The storm is real: it happened in May 2024 and the Curiosity rover measured it. The crew is imaginary: nobody lives on Mars yet.
inicio.paso1: Walk around the base and enter each module.
inicio.paso2: Share the power: there's never enough for everything.
inicio.paso3: Listen to your crew, but you decide.
inicio.paso4: When the storm arrives, everyone to the shelter!
